title: A 1% Investment Fee Can Cost You $120,000. Here's How
description:
Same plan, two funds: $10,000 to start plus $500 a month for 30 years. With a 0.05% yearly fee you'd end with about $687K. With a 1% fee, about $564K. The gap is about $123K: the fees plus the growth those fees would have earned. A fund's yearly fee is called its expense ratio, and it's listed on the fund's fact sheet.

Assumptions: 7% average yearly return before fees, compounded monthly; fees charged monthly as a share of the balance; no taxes or other costs. Illustration only: real returns vary and are not guaranteed. Not financial advice.

scenes.say: A one percent fee sounds tiny. On this plan, it could cost you over a hundred and twenty thousand dollars.
The plan: ten thousand dollars to start, plus five hundred a month, for thirty years.
Assume it earns seven percent a year before fees. Real returns vary.
Fund A charges five hundredths of a percent a year. Fund B charges one percent.
After thirty years: Fund A, nearly six hundred and ninety thousand. Fund B, about five hundred and sixty.
Fund B takes over sixty-two thousand in fees. Fund A, about thirty-six hundred.
That's over a hundred and twenty thousand dollars, gone to fees and the growth they took with them.
